The real L2 geometry and standard coordinate interpretation are part of the supplied context. theta, A, and f are literal local definitions, and lambda is notation abbreviating the displayed diagonal entry, not an additional hypothesis or choice.
conclusion: The conjunction is: (1) f is globally C-infinity, meaning continuous derivatives of every finite order; (2) for every x, the gradient map has a genuine real Frechet derivative h -> A*h at x; (3) f is strongly convex on all R^d with modulus 1, namely f(a*x+b*y)<=a*f(x)+b*f(y)-(a*b/2)*||x-y||^2 for nonnegative a,b summing to 1; (4) for every x,y, ||gradient f(x)-gradient f(y)||<=kappa*||x-y||; (5) f(0)=0; and (6) for every x, [for every y, f(x)<=f(y)] iff x=0. Hence the attained global minimum is unique at zero and has value zero.
constant_dependencies: d and kappa are universally chosen subject to their thresholds. theta depends on d and i; lambda depends on d,kappa,i; A depends on d,kappa,O; f depends on that A. The derivative map is the same A at every base point x. The strong-convexity modulus is exactly the stated 1, giving Jensen correction (a*b/2)*||x-y||^2. The global gradient Lipschitz bound uses the same input kappa, with coefficient exactly kappa. Both the dimension and kappa thresholds are 2. The function has the exact factor 1/2, its minimum value is exactly 0, and the minimizer is exactly the zero vector. No sharpness of the constants 1 or kappa is asserted.
domains: d is a natural number. kappa is a real number. O is a d-by-d real orthogonal matrix, allowing either determinant sign. The index i ranges over Fin d, identified with the integers 0 through d-1. Points and directions x,y,h are in real Euclidean R^d with the L2 norm. The strong-convexity weights a,b are real. f takes values in R. All function conclusions concern the full domain R^d.
objects: For I={0,...,d-1}, theta_i=((i+1/2)*pi)/d and lambda_i=(kappa+1)/2+((kappa-1)/2)*cos(theta_i). A=O*diag(lambda_i)*O^T. The real-valued function on Euclidean R^d is f(x)=(x^T*A*x)/2. Its gradient is interpreted using the standard real Euclidean Riesz identification. The matrix continuous linear map is h -> A*h.
quantifiers: For every d in N with d>=2, for every kappa in R with kappa>=2, and for every O in the full real orthogonal group of size d, make the displayed theta, lambda, A, and f definitions and assert all six conclusions simultaneously. The derivative-of-gradient assertion holds at every x in R^d, and the associated derivative acts as A on every direction h in R^d. The gradient norm bound holds for every x,y in R^d. Strong convexity means the displayed inequality for every x,y in R^d and every nonnegative real a,b with a+b=1. For every x in R^d, global minimization by x is equivalent to x=0; global minimization itself means f(x)<=f(y) for every y in R^d.

# Reconstructed mathematical proposition

For every natural number \(d\) with \(d\ge 2\), every real number \(\kappa\) with \(\kappa\ge 2\), and every real orthogonal \(d\times d\) matrix \(O\), use the index set \(I=\{0,1,\ldots,d-1\}\) and define
\[
\theta_i=\frac{(i+\tfrac12)\pi}{d},\qquad
\lambda_i=\frac{\kappa+1}{2}+\frac{\kappa-1}{2}\cos(\theta_i)
\quad(i\in I),
\]
\[
A=O\,\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i)_{i\in I}\,O^{\mathsf T},
\qquad
f:\mathbb R^d\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad
f(x)=\frac{x^{\mathsf T}Ax}{2}.
\]
Here \(\mathbb R^d\) has its standard real Euclidean inner product and norm, and orthogonality means \(O^{\mathsf T}O=OO^{\mathsf T}=I_d\), with either determinant sign allowed. All of the following conclusions hold together for these definitions:

1. The function \(f\) is globally \(C^\infty\): it has continuous derivatives of every finite order.
2. At every \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), the gradient map \(\nabla f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) has a genuine real Fréchet derivative equal to the linear map represented by \(A\). Explicitly, for every such \(x\),
   \[
   D(\nabla f)(x)[h]=Ah\qquad\text{for every }h\in\mathbb R^d.
   \]
3. The function \(f\) is strongly convex on all of \(\mathbb R^d\) with modulus \(1\). Explicitly, for every \(x,y\in\mathbb R^d\) and every \(a,b\in\mathbb R\) satisfying \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge0\), and \(a+b=1\),
   \[
   f(ax+by)\le a f(x)+b f(y)-\frac{ab}{2}\lVert x-y\rVert^2.
   \]
4. The gradient is globally Lipschitz with the stated bound \(\kappa\): for every \(x,y\in\mathbb R^d\),
   \[
   \lVert\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\rVert\le\kappa\lVert x-y\rVert.
   \]
5. \(f(0)=0\).
6. For every \(x\in\mathbb R^d\),
   \[
   \bigl(\text{for every }y\in\mathbb R^d,\ f(x)\le f(y)\bigr)
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=0.
   \]
   Thus the global minimum is attained uniquely at the zero vector, and its value is zero.

The formulas for \(\theta_i\), \(\lambda_i\), \(A\), and \(f\) are definitions inside the universal quantifiers, not additional hypotheses. The gradient uses the real Euclidean Riesz identification of the Fréchet derivative with a vector. Although the formal gradient operator is totalized, conclusion 1 supplies differentiability of \(f\), and conclusion 2 asserts actual derivative existence for the gradient at every point; a default value at a nondifferentiable point is not being used as evidence of differentiability. Smoothness here means every finite derivative order, without an analyticity assertion. The constants \(1\) and \(\kappa\) are the stated bounds; no assertion of their sharpness is included.
scopes: Every conclusion is inside the universal d,kappa,O quantifiers and uses the same locally defined theta,A,f. All spatial scopes are unrestricted R^d, not a neighborhood, trajectory, or bounded subset. The gradient is formally totalized, but global smoothness of f and the explicit HasFDerivAt statement give actual differentiability and actual derivative existence as specified; mere totalized values do not witness existence. C-infinity is not an analyticity claim. The minimizer biconditional has universal x scope and its minimum predicate has universal comparison-point y scope. There is no probability, random-matrix, algorithm, convergence, or complexity assertion.
